state.misconception_label: Ignores negative sign when expanding bracket

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: John is expanding these three brackets: \( (x+5)(x-3)(x+6) \) He finds it helpful to split the first bracket and view the problem as follows: \( x(x-3)(x+6)+5(x-3)(x+6) \) He expands the brackets further. Before he simplifies, what are the terms than contain an \( \boldsymbol{x}^{2} \) ? I got \( \begin{array}{l}+6 x^{2} \\ +3 x^{2} \\ +5 x^{2}\end{array} \) because I forgot that two negatives multiply to a positive.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think it's important to remember how negative signs interact when expanding brackets? Can you explain why you believe two negatives multiply to a positive in this context?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess it's important because if I don't remember that, I might get the wrong signs in my answers. Like, I thought \( -3 \) times \( -6 \) would just be \( +3 \) instead of \( +18 \) when I was expanding. Can you help me understand how to keep track of the negatives better?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a specific example where you encountered two negatives multiplying to a positive in a different context? How might that example help you remember to keep track of the negatives when expanding brackets in mathematics?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I remember in science class when we talked about how two negative charges repel each other, but if you think about it like multiplying, two negatives make a positive. I guess that’s kind of similar? But when I’m expanding brackets, I still get confused about when to apply the negatives. Can you explain again how to keep track of them when I’m multiplying?
